narrative:
Your predicted probability of leaving is 59.0%, so the model sees leaving as more likely than staying. Since a promotion is an investment in someone expected to remain, that prediction led to the denial.

The strongest signal was your overall experience of 1–5 years, which pushed toward staying and is the most common band among employees predicted to stay. The second strongest signal was that you reported no other job opportunities, which also reduced the likelihood of leaving. The third strongest was difficulty getting involved in your job—decision-making and having your opinions heard—which pushed toward leaving; employees predicted to stay more often found this medium or easy.

Those stay signals were outweighed by other concerns in your profile, including a low monthly salary of 1k–5k SAR, no medical insurance, no bonus, unpaid overtime, low job support, no recognition, no sense of job stability, low environment satisfaction, and general job dissatisfaction. Each adds to a picture of a workplace where leaving may feel attractive.

Before promotion is reconsidered, you and your manager should address involvement and voice at work, recognition and support, pay and overtime compensation, and job stability and satisfaction. You may also want to make your intention to stay explicit and agree on a development plan, while the organization should review whether these working conditions can be improved.
